source_text: Credimus etiam, quod sedet ad dexteram patris. nec ideo tamen quasi humana forma circumscriptum esse deum patrem arbitrandum est, ut de illo cogitantibus dextrum aut sinistrum latus animo occurrat; aut id ipsum, quod sedere pater dicitur, flexis poplitibus fieri putandum est, ne in illud incidamus sacrilegium, in quo exsecratur apostolus eos, qui commutauerunt gloriam incorruptibilis dei in similitudinem corruptibilis hominis. tale enim simulacrum deo nefas est christiano in templo conlocare; multo magis in corde nefarium est, ubi uere est templum dei, si a terrena cupiditate atque errore mundetur. ad dexteram ergo intellegendum est dictum esse (in summa beatitudine\', ubi iustitia, pax et gaudium est, sicut ad sinistram haedi constituuntur, id est in miseria, propter iniquitatis labores atque cruciatus. sedere ergo quod dicitur deus, non membrorum positionem, sed iudiciariam significat potestatem, qua illa maiestas numquam caret, semper dignis digna tribuendo, quamuis in extremo iudicio multo manifestius inter homines unigeniti filii dei iudicis uiuorum atque mortuorum claritas indubitata fulsura sit.
thought_title: Sitting at the right hand of the Father means judicial power, not bodily posture
orientation: Augustine is explaining the creed's clause that Christ sits at the Father's right hand, warning against imagining God in human bodily form.
pass_a_gloss: We believe also that he sits at the right hand of the Father. But not for that reason is God the Father to be thought of as bounded by human shape, so that to those thinking about him a right or left side occurs to the mind; nor is that very thing, that the Father is said to sit, to be thought to happen with bent knees, lest we fall into that sacrilege in which the apostle curses those who changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of a corruptible human. For it is wicked for a Christian to place such an image of God in a temple; much more is it wicked in the heart, where truly is the temple of God, if it is cleansed from earthly desire and error. Therefore it must be understood that it was said 'at the right hand' in the highest blessedness, where justice, peace and joy is, just as at the left hand the goats are placed, that is in misery, because of the labors and torments of iniquity. Therefore that God is said to sit does not signify a position of limbs, but judicial power, which that majesty never lacks, always giving worthy things to the worthy, although in the final judgment the undoubted brightness of the only Son of God, judge of the living and the dead, will shine much more manifestly among humans.

choices.english: at the right hand of the Father
choices.why: Standard rendering of the creedal phrase; 'right hand' keeps the spatial metaphor Augustine is explaining away.
rejected: on the right of the Father

choices.english: God the Father to be thought of as bounded by human shape
choices.why: Circumscriptum means enclosed or limited by a boundary; 'bounded' preserves the spatial sense Augustine denies.
Literal rendering of the ablative absolute; Augustine is mocking a bodily picture of sitting.

choices.english: into the likeness of a corruptible human
choices.why: Echoes Romans 1:23 wording; 'corruptible human' keeps the contrast with 'incorruptible God.'
rejected: into the image of a mortal man
into the likeness of corruptible man

choices.why: Iudiciariam is an adjective meaning 'pertaining to judgment'; 'judicial power' captures the legal sense Augustine assigns to sitting.
Summa means highest or supreme; 'blessedness' renders beatitudo as the state of blessed happiness.

bible_refs.note: commutauerunt gloriam incorruptibilis dei in similitudinem corruptibilis hominis

pass_b_english: We also believe that he sits at the right hand of the Father. But this does not mean we should think of God the Father as bounded by human shape, so that when we think of him a right or left side comes to mind. Nor should we suppose that when the Father is said to sit, he does so with bent knees. Otherwise we fall into the sacrilege for which the apostle curses those who changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of a corruptible human (Romans 1:23). It is wicked for a Christian to set up such an image of God in a temple; it is far more wicked to set it up in the heart, where the temple of God truly is, once it has been cleansed of earthly desire and error. So we must understand “at the right hand” as meaning in the highest blessedness, where justice, peace, and joy are. In the same way, the goats are placed at the left (Matthew 25:33), that is, in misery, because of the labors and torments of wickedness. Therefore when God is said to sit, this does not signify a position of bodily parts but judicial power. That majesty is never without this power, always giving to each what each deserves, although at the final judgment the unmistakable glory of the only Son of God, the judge of the living and the dead, will shine far more openly among human beings.

last_rejected.quote: always giving to each what each deserves
last_rejected.why: 'dignis digna' = 'to the worthy, worthy things' or 'to each what they deserve.' But 'dignis' is dative plural = 'to the worthy/deserving ones.' The English 'to each what each deserves' loses the sense that God gives 'worthy things' to 'worthy persons'—there's a double dignity. More importantly, 'dignis' implies God gives according to desert/merit, which is a key theological point about divine justice.
last_rejected.fix: always rendering to the worthy what is worthy
last_rejected.ruling: 'dignis digna tribuendo' = giving worthy things to worthy persons; 'to each what each deserves' conveys same meaning adequately.

last_rejected.quote: the judge of the living and the dead
last_rejected.why: English says 'the judge of the living and the dead' but this is in genitive: 'of the only-begotten Son of God, of the judge of the living and the dead' or 'the only-begotten Son of God, judge of the living and the dead.' The English makes 'judge' in apposition to 'Son,' but the Latin has 'iudicis' genitive, dependent on 'claritas' or in parallel with 'filii dei'—actually 'unigeniti filii dei iudicis uiuorum atque mortuorum' = 'of the only-begotten Son of God, judge of the living and the dead.' This is a genitive chain: 'the glory of the only-begotten Son of God, judge of the living and the dead.' The English 'the only Son of God, the judge of the living and the dead' makes 'judge' nominative in apposition, but Latin has genitive 'iudicis.' This changes the grammatical construction but does it change meaning? The glory belongs to the Son who is judge. The English 'the glory of the only Son of God, the judge of the living and the dead' could be read as 'the glory of [the only Son of God, the judge...]' which is the same sense. Actually, re-reading English: 'the unmistakable glory of the only Son of God, the judge of the living and the dead'—this is ambiguous: is 'the judge' in apposition to 'Son' or separate? In English, the comma makes it apposition. But in Latin, 'iudicis' is genitive, so 'of the only-begotten Son of God, of the judge...' or 'of the only-begotten Son of God, judge...' The English rendering with comma + 'the judge' is standard literary translation for this kind of construction. Not an error.
last_rejected.ruling: English appositive 'the judge' correctly renders genitive 'iudicis' dependent on 'claritas'; meaning unchanged, standard rendering.
